# Overview

In Exercise 7, accessibility to eldercare centres was measured from the distances between hexagons and centres. In this exercise, the distances between villages and stores are used to divide the residents of Taichung City, Taiwan, among the 28 stores of a fast-food franchise.

On slide 6, the Huff model "estimates the probability of a consumer visiting a specific store by considering the store's attractiveness and the distance to it, relative to competing stores". The probabilities define the trade area of each store. Multiplied by the population of each village and summed over the villages, the probabilities give an estimate of the customers of each store.

This exercise is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 18, which computes the Huff probabilities with the `MCI` package, maps the trade area of one store and compares the estimated customers of each store with its recorded sales.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Sources

The hands-on exercise for Lesson 8 is this chapter:

- [Chapter 18: Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations using Huff model](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap18.html)

The Lesson 8 outline lists readings for before the lesson. Three are used here.

| Reading | What it contributes | Used in |
|----|----|----|
| **Rodrigue**, *The Geography of Transport Systems*, A.18 "Spatial Interactions and the Gravity Model" | The general spatial interaction model $T_{ij} = f(V_i, W_j, S_{ij})$, with $S_{ij}$ the "friction of distance" | 3.1 |
| **Rodrigue**, *The Geography of Transport Systems*, A.15 "Market Area Analysis" | Market areas as "ranges of probabilities that customers will attend specific locations (Huff's law)"; the two-store figure of slide 7 | 3.1 |
| **Huff (1963)**, "A Probabilistic Analysis of Shopping Center Trade Areas" | The model, with selling space as attraction and travel time as cost; an exponent estimated from data | 3.1 |

Of the eight references the outline also lists, the following is used on this page:

| Reference | What it contributes | Used in |
|----|----|----|
| **Wieland (2017)**, "Market Area Analysis for Retail and Service Locations with MCI" | The functions of the `MCI` package | 3.1 |

The other references are about gravity models of flows between regions (Haynes and Fotheringham, 2020; Farmer and Oshan, 2017; Flowerdew and Aitkin, 1982; Klapka et al., 2013; Yue et al., 2012) and spatial econometric models of origin-destination flows (Floch and Le Saout, 2018; LeSage and Pace, 2008; Tsutsumi and Tamesue, 2012). Chapter 18 has no flow data, so these references are background reading for this page. The outline's "All About R" section links `MCI` and `REAT`. `MCI` is used throughout. `REAT` also has a `huff()` function, which this page does not use.

The Lesson 8 slide deck (the version of 24 October 2026) has 13 slides. Slide 5 gives Reilly's law. Slides 6 and 7 introduce the Huff model, and slides 8 and 9 give its utility and probability. Slides 10 and 11 give the expected customers and the market share of each store. Slides 12 and 13 give the MCI model.
:::

## The data

The data sets are distributed with the exercise on eLearn, in the folder `data/`.

| Data set | Format | Features | Contents |
|----|----|----|----|
| `STORES_TC` | ESRI shapefile | 28 points | stores of the franchise in Taichung City, with name, address and store code |
| `TOWN_TC` | ESRI shapefile | 28 polygons | districts of Taichung City |
| `VILLAGE_TC` | ESRI shapefile | 622 polygons | villages (里) of Taichung City, with the village code `VILLCODE` |
| `pop2019.csv` | CSV | 625 rows | households (`H_CNT`), population (`P_CNT`), males (`M_CNT`) and females (`F_CNT`) of each village, December 2019 |
| `Store_sales_data.csv` | CSV | 5,499 rows | number of bills and sales amount (currency not given) by store code and `POD code` |

The folder also has `storeCD.csv` and a second store layer, `STORES_TC1`, which the chapter does not use. `storeCD.csv` gives each of the 28 stores the same `Capacity`, 50, with no unit. `STORES_TC1` has the 28 stores and a 29th point, "New Store", with the code `NS`.

## Geospatial data

### Reading the three layers

```{.r .cell-code}
                  layer = "STORES_TC")
town <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                layer = "TOWN_TC")
village <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                   layer = "VILLAGE_TC")
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

       features = c(nrow(stores), nrow(town), nrow(village)),
       geometry = c(as.character(st_geometry_type(stores, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(town, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(village, by_geometry = FALSE))),
       epsg = c(st_crs(stores)$epsg, st_crs(town)$epsg, st_crs(village)$epsg)) |>
```

``` r
st_geometry_type(x, by_geometry = FALSE)                  # sf
```

- `st_read()` reads the shapefile named by `layer` from the folder `dsn` into a simple feature data frame. `results: hide` suppresses the report that `st_read()` prints for each file.

- `tibble()` builds a data frame with one row for each layer, and `kable()` prints it as a table. The other tables on this page are also printed with `kable()`. Where `digits` is given, it rounds the numbers.

The three layers are in TWD97 / TM2 zone 121, EPSG:3826, a projected coordinate system in metres, so distances between the layers can be computed without a transformation.

- `TOWNENG` holds the English name of each district, such as "Xitun District". `str_remove()` drops " District", and `recode()` writes out the short names of the five central districts, such as "W." for West and "Zhong" for Central.
- The five central districts cover 0.9 to 7.8 km² each, too small for a name on the map of the whole city. The dashed rectangle marks them on the first map, and the second map shows them at a larger scale.
- `label_point()` finds a place for the name of a district. `st_make_grid()` puts points 250 m apart over the district, and the function keeps the point farthest from both the district boundary and the nearest store, so that the name lies inside its district and clear of the store labels.

- Each `tm_shape()` starts a layer, and the layers are drawn in order: the villages in grey, the district boundaries in blue, the district names in blue italics, and the stores as red points.
- `tm_text()` writes the store code of each point. `ymod` moves the label up so that it does not cover the point.
- Each layer is drawn in one colour, so `tm_add_legend()` adds one legend entry for each layer.
- `tm_compass()`, `tm_scalebar()` and `tm_grid()` add a north arrow, a scale bar and grid lines with coordinates in metres. `legend.outside = TRUE` places the legend outside the map frame: to the right of the map, or below it when the legend is too wide for the space on the right.

## Data preparation

### Aggregating store sales


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
store_sales_aggre <- store_sales |>
  group_by(`Store Code`) |>
  summarise(Total_Bill = sum(Bills, na.rm = TRUE),
            Total_Sales = sum(Amount, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
``` r
group_by(x, ...); summarise(...)                          # dplyr
```

- `group_by()` groups the rows by store code, and `summarise()` returns one row for each store code, with the sum of the bills and the sum of the sales amount over all its `POD code` rows.
- The backticks around `` `Store Code` `` are needed because the column name contains a space.
:::

### Relational join


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
stores <- stores |>
  left_join(store_sales_aggre,
            by = join_by(Store_CD == `Store Code`))

stores_tidied <- stores |>
  mutate(Store_size = 1) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

summary(stores)
```


- `left_join()` keeps the 28 rows of `stores` and adds the total bills and sales of the row of `store_sales_aggre` whose `Store Code` equals the store's `Store_CD`. The rows of `store_sales_aggre` with store codes that are not in `stores` are dropped.

- The data have no size for the stores, so the attraction is the same constant for every store. The chapter uses 100. The constant cancels from the probabilities of `huff.shares()`: with `Store_size = 1` and `Store_size = 100`, the 17,276 values of `p_ij` differ by less than $10^{-15}$. The value 1 does not look like a measured size, which 100 can.
:::

The household size has a correlation of -0.3 with the household count and -0.16 with the population, so it can replace the household count. The population stays for the size of the village, and the household size describes its composition.

A principal component analysis would also remove the correlation, but its components are mixtures of the original variables, and a component such as "0.7 population + 0.7 households" cannot be explained for a village. The household size is a ratio with a meaning, people per household, so it is used instead.

# Part 1: Chapter 18

## The Huff model

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## The model of Huff (1963)

In "Spatial Interactions and the Gravity Model", section A.18 of the Methods chapter of *The Geography of Transport Systems*, Rodrigue writes the general spatial interaction model as

$$\begin{aligned}
T_{ij} &= f(V_i, W_j, S_{ij}) \\
&= f(\text{attributes of origin } i, \ \text{attributes of destination } j, \ \text{friction of distance from } i \text{ to } j)
\end{aligned}$$

where $T_{ij}$ is the interaction between origin $i$ and destination $j$. In the Huff model, the attribute of the destination is the attraction of a store and the friction is the distance to it.

**Reilly's law (slide 5).** Reilly's law of retail gravitation (1931) finds the point of indifference between two locations, which divides their trading areas. On the slide, two locations are 75 km apart. If the two were equal, the point would lie halfway, 37.5 km from each. Location A has the larger population, so it draws more customers and the point lies 45.9 km from A.

Huff (1963, p. 82) traces the breaking point to the "Law of Retail Gravitation" of Reilly (1929): a town between two cities divides its trade between them "in direct proportion to the populations of the two cities and in inverse proportion to the square of the distances". In the notation of Huff,

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{B_a}{B_b} &= \frac{P_a}{P_b} \left(\frac{D_b}{D_a}\right)^2 \\[4pt]
&= \frac{\text{population of city } a}{\text{population of city } b} \times \left(\frac{\text{distance from the town to city } b}{\text{distance from the town to city } a}\right)^2
\end{aligned}$$

where $B_a$ and $B_b$ are the proportions of the trade of the town attracted by cities $a$ and $b$. The breaking point is the town where $B_a = B_b$, which Huff calls "the .5 probability position between two cities". With the squared distance, the breaking point lies $D_{ab} / (1 + \sqrt{P_a /
P_b})$ from city $b$, where $D_{ab}$ is the distance between the two cities. For the slide, with populations of 250,000 and 100,000, the point lies $75 / (1 + \sqrt{250{,}000 / 100{,}000}) = 29.1$ km from the smaller location and $75 - 29.1 = 45.9$ km from A. The figure of slide 7 divides by the distance itself, not by its square. Rodrigue (A.15) lists Reilly's law as the step at which "market size" entered market area analysis. Wieland (2017, p. 298) calls these early models deterministic: "each customer origin is assigned completely to one supply location".

In the Huff model, the ratio of Reilly is extended to any number of stores, with a probability for each store. With two stores and $\lambda = 2$, the ratio $p_{ia} / p_{ib}$ of the Huff model below is the ratio $B_a / B_b$ of Reilly.

Huff (1963, p. 86) gives the probability that consumers in statistical unit $i$ travel to shopping centre $j$ as the selling space of $j$ divided by a power of the travel time from $i$ to $j$, relative to the same ratio for every centre. On slides 8 and 9, in the notation of Wieland (2017, p. 299), the utility of store $j$ for the customers of origin $i$ is

$$\begin{aligned}
U_{ij} &= A_j^{\gamma} \, d_{ij}^{-\lambda} \\
&= \frac{(\text{attraction of store } j)^{\gamma}}{(\text{distance from village } i \text{ to store } j)^{\lambda}}
\end{aligned}$$

and the probability that the customers of $i$ choose $j$ is

$$\begin{aligned}
p_{ij} &= \frac{U_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} U_{ik}} = \frac{A_j^{\gamma} \, d_{ij}^{-\lambda}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} A_k^{\gamma} \, d_{ik}^{-\lambda}} \\[6pt]
&= \frac{(\text{attraction of store } j)^{\gamma} \div (\text{distance from village } i \text{ to store } j)^{\lambda}}{\text{sum over all } n \text{ stores } k \text{ of } (\text{attraction of store } k)^{\gamma} \div (\text{distance from village } i \text{ to store } k)^{\lambda}}
\end{aligned}$$

where $A_j$ is the attraction of store $j$, $d_{ij}$ is the distance or travel time, $\gamma$ is the weight of the attraction and $\lambda$ is the weight of the distance. The probabilities of one origin sum to 1.

On slide 10, the expected number of customers from $i$ at $j$ is

$$\begin{aligned}
E_{ij} &= p_{ij} \, C_i \\
&= (\text{probability of store } j \text{ for village } i) \times (\text{market potential of village } i)
\end{aligned}$$

where the market potential $C_i$ is the number of potential customers or the purchasing power in village $i$. On slide 11, the expected customers of store $j$ in the whole study area and the market share of store $j$ are

$$\begin{aligned}
T_j &= \sum_{i} E_{ij} \\
&= \text{sum over all villages } i \text{ of the expected customers from } i \text{ at store } j
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
M_j &= \frac{T_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} T_k} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{\text{expected customers of store } j}{\text{expected customers of all } n \text{ stores}}
\end{aligned}$$

The symbols of the formulas, and the columns that hold them in the code of this page:

| Symbol | Meaning | Column |
|----|----|----|
| $i$ | origin: a village | `VILLCODE` |
| $j$, $k$ | a store | `Store_CD` |
| $n$ | number of stores: 28 |  |
| $A_j$ | attraction of store $j$ | `Store_size` |
| $d_{ij}$ | distance from village $i$ to store $j$, in metres | `distance` |
| $\gamma$, $\lambda$ | weights of the attraction and the distance | arguments `gamma` and `lambda` |
| $U_{ij}$ | utility of store $j$ for the residents of village $i$ | `U_ij` |
| $p_{ij}$ | probability that a resident of village $i$ chooses store $j$ | `p_ij` |
| $C_i$ | market potential of village $i$: its residents | `P_CNT` |
| $E_{ij}$ | expected customers from village $i$ at store $j$ | computed in `shares.total()` |
| $T_j$ | expected customers of store $j$ | `sum_E_j` |
| $M_j$ | market share of store $j$ | `share_j` |

`huff.shares()` of the `MCI` package writes the decay as $d_{ij}^{\lambda}$ with a negative `lambda`. Its default `lambda = -2` corresponds to $\lambda = 2$ in the formula above.

In panel 1, the two distances are equal, so $37.5^2$ cancels from the fraction and the shares are in the ratio of the sizes: $250{,}000 \div 350{,}000 = 0.71$. Rodrigue's figure divides by the distance itself ($\lambda = 1$) and gives the same 0.71, because the exponent has no effect when the two distances are equal. In panel 2, the two sizes are equal, so the size cancels and the shares depend on the distances only: store a, at half the distance of store b, has four times the utility of store b. Every store in chapter 18 has the same size, so the model of this exercise works as in panel 2.
:::

The usual choice for the point of a polygon is the centroid, the centre of mass of its shape. The last column shows its weakness: the centroid of a polygon with a concave or an odd shape can fall outside the polygon, as for Yong'an Village. ## Trade areas of all stores

The map of store BT shows the probabilities of one store. To give every village to one store, the probabilities of the 28 stores of a village are compared, and the store with the highest probability is the most likely store of the village. The villages of a store form its trade area.

`huff_share` is in long format, with one row for each pair of village and store, so that the 28 probabilities of a village stand in 28 rows. The comparison is simpler with one row for each village and one column for each store, so the table is first made wider.

```{.r .cell-code}
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD,

```

The next chunk adds the column `TA`, for trade area. For each village, it compares the 28 values of the row and takes the store with the highest value, so `TA` holds the code of the store whose trade area the village belongs to.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
huff_TA <- huff_share_wider |>
  mutate(TA = names(pick(2:29))[max.col(pick(2:29), ties.method = "first")])

huff_TA_tidied <- huff_TA |>
  select(VILLCODE, TA)
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
``` r
pivot_wider(df, names_from, values_from)                  # tidyr
pick(...); max.col(m, ties.method)                        # dplyr, base R
```

- `pivot_wider()` is the reverse of `pivot_longer()`: the values of `Store_CD` become 28 columns, and each village is one row.
- `pick(2:29)` selects the 28 store columns inside `mutate()`. Column 1 is `VILLCODE`.
- `max.col()` returns, for each row, the position of the largest value among the 28 columns. `ties.method = "first"` takes the first column when two values are equal.
- `names(pick(2:29))[...]` turns each position into the store code of that column, and `mutate()` stores it in `TA`: the trade area is compared across the 28 values, and the highest one is taken.
- `huff_TA_tidied` keeps the village code and `TA`, so that the 28 probability columns are not carried into the join with the village polygons.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" title="Why huff_TA_tidied is a separate step"}
`huff_TA_tidied` returns only `VILLCODE` and `TA`, so that the table is simple: the 28 probability columns are not needed after the comparison, and the join with the village polygons adds one column instead of 29. The steps are written separately here so that each result can be looked at. They can also be written as one pipe, with the tidying nested in the step of `huff_TA`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
huff_TA_tidied <- huff_share_wider |>
  mutate(TA = names(pick(2:29))[max.col(pick(2:29), ties.method = "first")]) |>
  select(VILLCODE, TA)
```
:::


The result is the same table. The village polygons are then joined with it: `village_TA <- village |> left_join(huff_TA_tidied, by = join_by(VILLCODE))`. Both tables have the village code under the same name, so `join_by(VILLCODE)` is enough.
:::

::::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" title="A larger trade area is not a larger market share"}
The size of the coloured area on the map is not the size of the market of the store. A large area can be sparse: it has few residents for its size, so the store has few potential customers there. A small area can be compact, with many residents close to the store, so the store has more customers and the distance to each of them is short. For a delivery service, a compact area means a short travel distance for each order. The market of a store is the sum of the expected customers of its villages, $T_j$ of section 3.6, and not the area of its villages.
